explanations.explanation: Only the high priest goes through that second curtain. The other priests handle the first room, where the lampstand, the table and the consecrated bread are. The second room, the Most Holy Place, is his alone. That's a very short guest list, friend.

I see where that comes from, because the priests DO go in regularly. But the text says they enter the first room to do their sacred duties. The second room is different: only the high priest goes in there. One name on the list, baker.

The elders don't show up in this passage at all. The writer names two kinds of visitors. The priests go into the first room, and only the high priest enters the second. So that Most Holy Place stays closed to everybody else.

Blood it is. The writer says the high priest never entered without it, and he offered it for himself and for the sins the people had committed in ignorance (Hebrews 9:7). He didn't just show up and hope for the best. Only the high priest went into that second room, and only once a year.

Oil doesn't come up in this passage. The writer says the high priest never entered without blood. That's what he offered for himself and for the sins the people had committed in ignorance. Easy to mix up when you're picturing a whole room full of sacred things.

Water is close to something in the passage, because special washings come up later in verse 10. But those are called external regulations. What the high priest never went in without was blood. He offered it for himself and for the sins the people had committed in ignorance.

True, and notice who's doing the showing: the Holy Spirit. The writer says that by this arrangement, the way into the Most Holy Place had not yet been disclosed as long as the first tabernacle was still standing. So the tabernacle itself was showing something. I think that's worth a second look.

The text says the opposite. By this arrangement, the Holy Spirit was showing that the way into the Most Holy Place had not yet been disclosed while the first tabernacle was still standing. So this statement is true. The whole setup was pointing to something.

That's it. The writer says the gifts and sacrifices were unable to cleanse the conscience of the worshiper. They dealt with outside things, but the inside was still waiting. Keep that one in your apron pocket, because it comes back in a big way later in this passage.

Earning a priesthood isn't what the writer is talking about. Nobody is shopping for a promotion in this passage. The limit he names is that these gifts and sacrifices were unable to cleanse the conscience of the worshiper.

A long life isn't mentioned anywhere in this passage. The writer's point is about the inside of a person. The gifts and sacrifices were unable to cleanse the conscience of the worshiper. That's the limit he names.

These rules weren't meant to stay forever. The writer calls them external regulations imposed until the time of reform. That phrase has a finish line built right into it. So this one is false: they were for a set time, not for always.

False is right. The writer says these were external regulations imposed until the time of reform. A rule that's imposed until a certain time has an end date. So they weren't meant to stay in place forever.

explanations.answer: A greater one not made by hands
explanations.explanation: Yes, a greater and more perfect tabernacle, one that is not made by hands and is not a part of this creation. The writer says Christ went through it as high priest of the good things that have come. That's the tabernacle in verse 11. Quite a contrast with the earthly sanctuary in verse 1.

explanations.answer: A grander one built of gold
explanations.explanation: Gold shows up in this passage, but it belongs to the earthly tabernacle, like the gold-covered ark and the gold jar of manna. The tabernacle Christ goes through is greater and more perfect. The writer says it is not made by hands and is not a part of this creation. Gold isn't part of how he describes it.

explanations.answer: A larger one built on Zion
explanations.explanation: Zion isn't mentioned in this passage. The writer says Christ went through the greater and more perfect tabernacle that is not made by hands and is not a part of this creation. That's how the text describes it. A place on a map isn't part of that description.

By His own blood. The writer says Christ did not enter by the blood of goats and calves, but entered the Most Holy Place once for all by His own blood, thus securing eternal redemption. That's the big contrast with the high priest, who offered blood for himself and for the people (Hebrews 9:7). Christ entered by His own.

Bulls do come up in this passage, but on the old side of things. Verse 13 mentions the blood of goats and bulls for making bodies ceremonially clean. Verse 12 says Christ entered by His own blood. That's the big contrast.

Doves don't come up in this passage. The animals the writer names are goats, calves, bulls and a heifer, all on the old side of things. Christ entered the Most Holy Place by His own blood. That's what secured eternal redemption.

The yearly trip is the high priest's pattern, not Christ's. The writer says the high priest entered the second room only once a year. Christ entered the Most Holy Place once for all. So no return trips are needed. This one is false.
False is right. The high priest went in once a year, but Christ entered the Most Holy Place once for all by His own blood. One entry, and redemption secured. No yearly schedule needed.

Eternal. The writer says Christ entered once for all by His own blood, thus securing eternal redemption. The high priest went in once a year, but Christ entered once for all. That's the redemption He secured.
Yearly is the old pattern. The high priest went into the second room only once a year. But Christ entered once for all and secured eternal redemption. That's redemption with no expiration date.
Partial isn't the word the writer uses. Christ entered the Most Holy Place once for all by His own blood, thus securing eternal redemption. The word is eternal. That's what the text says He secured.

Christ Himself. The writer says that through the eternal Spirit, He offered Himself unblemished to God. He is the one who offered, and He offered Himself. That's why His blood can purify our consciences from works of death, so that we may serve the living God.
Angels aren't mentioned in this passage. The writer says Christ, through the eternal Spirit, offered Himself unblemished to God. Nobody else is named as the one offering.

The priests on earth are all on the old side of this passage, going into the first room to do their sacred duties. For Christ, the writer says He offered Himself unblemished to God through the eternal Spirit. So it wasn't earthly priests who offered Him.

True. The writer says the blood of Christ will purify our consciences from works of death, so that we may serve the living God. It cleans us on the inside, and it points us toward serving. Compare that to the old gifts, which couldn't do this.
The text says it is true. The blood of Christ will purify our consciences from works of death, so that we may serve the living God. That purpose is stated right in the verse. So the statement holds.
